title: survey-weighted-analyses
text:
Preface
This book walks through a complete analysis of complex survey data in R, from downloading the raw file to reporting a multivariable model:
It is written for students who know some R and the basics of regression, and who are new to survey weights or multiple imputation.

title: survey-weighted-analyses
text:
The question
Is household income associated with diabetes among US adults? Diabetes is common, costly, and unequally distributed. Income shapes access to healthy food, safe places to be active, health care, and the time and resources to manage a chronic condition. We estimate how the prevalence of diabetes differs across income groups, before and after accounting for age, sex, and race and ethnicity. An exercise in 6  Multivariable Models repeats the analysis for fair or poor general health.

title: survey-weighted-analyses
text:
The data
We use the 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS): telephone interviews with 457,670 adults, weighted to represent the US adult population. The data are public. You download them yourself (1  Importing the Data) and they stay on your computer.

title: survey-weighted-analyses
text:
Setup

Install R (version 4.6.1 was used to build this book), Quarto, and an editor such as RStudio or Positron.
Open the project: double-click survey-weighted-analyses.Rproj (RStudio) or open the folder (Positron).
Install the packages: in the R console, run renv::restore(). This installs the exact package versions the book was built with into the project (see Appendix B — Reproducibility).
For interactive chunks, run setwd("book") in the R console first. Download the data by opening book/01-import.qmd and running the download chunk once.

Then render the book from the terminal with quarto render book (the result is book/_book/index.html), or run the chapters’ code chunk by chunk, in order. Each chapter saves what the next one needs in data/processed/. Rendering time depends on available memory, processor cores and the number of imputations.
The import, survey tables, imputations and model fits reuse cached calculations on subsequent renders (see Calculate once, then reuse and Appendix B — Reproducibility). For descriptive statistics alone, run Chapters 1–3 and stop there.
For a quick test of the whole pipeline, quarto render book --profile smoke uses 2 imputations instead of 5 and writes to separate folders (book/_book-smoke/, data/processed-smoke/), so it never replaces the real results.

text:
How the code is written

Every function is called with its package name, as in dplyr::mutate(), so you always know where a function comes from (and packages cannot silently mask each other).
|> is R’s pipe: x |> f() means f(x).
Lines that start with # Check: stop the code with an error if an assumption about the data fails. A silent check means the data are as expected.
tidylog:: versions of dplyr verbs print what each step did (rows dropped, variables created, share missing).

title: 1  Importing the Data
text:
1.1 The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System
The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) is the largest continuously running health survey in the world. Every year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the states interview hundreds of thousands of US adults by landline and cell phone about their health conditions, health behaviors, and use of health care. In 2024, 457,670 adults in 49 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the US Virgin Islands completed the interview (Tennessee did not collect enough data to be included).
BRFSS is a complex survey:
Every estimate in this book uses all three. Chapter 3 shows what happens when they are ignored.

title: 1  Importing the Data
text:
Strata. Each state’s sample is drawn separately within strata (for example, by region and by landline or cell phone).
Primary sampling units (PSUs). Within a stratum, phone numbers are sampled. In BRFSS each respondent is their own PSU.
Weights. People are sampled with different probabilities and respond at different rates. CDC’s final weight (_LLCPWT) corrects for both and makes the weighted sample match each state’s adult population by age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and other characteristics (“raking”).

title: 1  Importing the Data
text:
1.2 Download the data (run once)
CDC distributes the data as a zipped SAS transport file (.XPT), a format that stores a SAS dataset in a portable way. The zip file is 83 MB, and the unzipped file is 1.1 GB.
Run the chunk below once, by hand (it is not run when the book is rendered). It saves data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT. Raw data, processed data and caches are excluded from Git.


Code
dir.create("../data/raw", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
zip_file <- "../data/raw/LLCP2024XPT.zip"
options(timeout = 600) # allow 10 minutes on a slow connection
utils::download.file(
  "https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/files/LLCP2024XPT.zip",
  destfile = zip_file,
  mode = "wb"
)
# The zip file names its contents "LLCP2024.XPT " (with a trailing space), so rename the file.
extracted <- utils::unzip(zip_file, exdir = "../data/raw")
file.rename(extracted, "../data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT")
file.remove(zip_file)








TipDownloading by hand



You can also download the zip file from the CDC BRFSS 2024 page (“2024 BRFSS Data (SAS Transport Format)”), unzip it, and save the file as data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT. The same page has the codebook, which lists every variable, its question, and its codes.

title: 2  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
2.1 Step 1: Declare what each item can be
Raw BRFSS answers are numeric codes. Cleaning turns them into labeled categories that R and readers understand. It is also where most analysis errors start: a code that slips through unrecoded (a 99 for “refused” read as an income group) or a missing value silently turned into “no” changes every result that follows.
This chapter follows four rules:
The values below come from the BRFSS 2024 codebook. BRFSS uses the same codes for non-answers throughout: 7 (or 77) for “Don’t know/Not sure”, 9 (or 99) for “Refused”, and a blank (NA in R) for “Not asked or missing”.
Code
# Possible values of each item in the BRFSS 2024 codebook. Blank (NA) means "not asked or
# missing".
item_values <- list(
  DIABETE4 = c(1:4, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 Yes, but only during pregnancy; 3 No;
  # 4 No, prediabetes or borderline; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  GENHLTH = c(1:5, 7, 9), # 1 Excellent; 2 Very good; 3 Good; 4 Fair; 5 Poor;
  # 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  MEDCOST1 = c(1, 2, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 No; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  INCOME3 = c(1:11, 77, 99), # 1 Less than $10,000 ... 11 $200,000 or more;
  # 77 Don't know; 99 Refused
  `_AGE_G` = 1:6, # 1 18-24; 2 25-34; 3 35-44; 4 45-54; 5 55-64; 6 65+
  `_AGE80` = 18:80, # CDC-imputed age in years; 80 means 80 or older
  SEXVAR = 1:2, # 1 Male; 2 Female
  `_IMPRACE` = 1:6, # 1 White; 2 Black; 3 Asian; 4 American Indian or Alaska
  # Native (all non-Hispanic); 5 Hispanic; 6 Other, non-Hispanic
  EDUCA = c(1:6, 9), # 1 Never attended ... 6 College 4 years or more; 9 Refused
  EMPLOY1 = 1:9, # 1 Employed for wages ... 8 Unable to work; 9 Refused
  `_STATE` = c(1, 2, 4:6, 8:13, 15:42, 44:46, 48:51, 53:56, 66, 72, 78) # FIPS codes
)
# The design variables and the CDC-imputed items are never blank.
never_blank <- c(
  "_LLCPWT",
  "_STSTR",
  "_PSU",
  "_STATE",
  "_AGE_G",
  "_AGE80",
  "SEXVAR",
  "_IMPRACE"
)
The 53 state codes are the 2024 codebook’s: the 50 states except Tennessee (47), plus the District of Columbia (11), Guam (66), Puerto Rico (72), and the US Virgin Islands (78).

section: 2.2 Step 2: Check the data against the codebook
text:
2.2 Step 2: Check the data against the codebook
A codebook can be wrong, and a file can change between releases. This check compares every observed value with the declaration and stops, naming each item and value, if anything else appears. It is silent when the data are as declared.


Code
# Check: every value is in the codebook.
unexpected <- purrr::imap(item_values, \(values, item) {
  setdiff(brfss[[item]], c(values, NA))
}) |>
  purrr::compact()
if (length(unexpected) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Values not in the codebook: ",
    paste0(
      names(unexpected),
      " (",
      purrr::map_chr(unexpected, toString),
      ")",
      collapse = "; "
    )
  )
}
# Check: no blanks where the codebook has none, and every weight is positive.
stopifnot(!anyNA(brfss[never_blank]), all(brfss[["_LLCPWT"]] > 0))

title: 2  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
2.3 Step 3: Recode
dplyr::recode_values() maps each code (left of ~) to a value (right of ~). With unmatched = "error", any code we did not list stops the run, so nothing can slip through. tidylog::mutate() works like dplyr::mutate() but reports what each new variable looks like, including its share of missing values.
Four decisions are built into this recoding (Appendix A lists them with counts):

Non-answers become missing. “Don’t know”, “refused”, and blank tell us nothing about a person’s true value, so they become NA. Chapter 4 fills them in by multiple imputation rather than dropping those people.
Values that other answers settle are coded, not left missing. A woman told she had diabetes only during pregnancy (DIABETE4 = 2) does not have diabetes now, so she is coded “No”.
Age and race and ethnicity come from CDC’s imputed versions. CDC fills the few missing answers for these weighting variables (_AGE_G, _IMPRACE), so they are never blank. Six age groups adjust for age much better than two.
Reference groups come first. The first level of each factor is the comparison group in the models: the lowest income group, ages 18-24, female, and non-Hispanic White (the largest group).



Code
brfss_clean <- brfss |>
  tidylog::mutate(
    diabetes = dplyr::recode_values(
      DIABETE4,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      c(2, 3) ~ "No", # 2 = told only during pregnancy: no diabetes now
      4 ~ "Prediabetes",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Prediabetes", "Yes")),
    genhlth = dplyr::recode_values(
      GENHLTH,
      1 ~ "Excellent",
      2 ~ "Very good",
      3 ~ "Good",
      4 ~ "Fair",
      5 ~ "Poor",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Excellent", "Very good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor")),
    cost_barrier = dplyr::recode_values(
      MEDCOST1,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      2 ~ "No",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    income = dplyr::recode_values(
      INCOME3,
      1:4 ~ "Less than $25,000",
      5:6 ~ "$25,000 to $49,999",
      7:8 ~ "$50,000 to $99,999",
      9:11 ~ "$100,000 or more",
      c(77, 99, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than $25,000",
          "$25,000 to $49,999",
          "$50,000 to $99,999",
          "$100,000 or more"
        )
      ),
    age_group = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_AGE_G`,
      1 ~ "18-24",
      2 ~ "25-34",
      3 ~ "35-44",
      4 ~ "45-54",
      5 ~ "55-64",
      6 ~ "65 or older",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65 or older")
      ),
    age = as.numeric(`_AGE80`),
    sex = dplyr::recode_values(
      SEXVAR,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    race_eth = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_IMPRACE`,
      1 ~ "Non-Hispanic White",
      2 ~ "Non-Hispanic Black",
      3 ~ "Non-Hispanic Asian",
      4 ~ "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
      5 ~ "Hispanic",
      6 ~ "Non-Hispanic other race",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Non-Hispanic White",
          "Non-Hispanic Black",
          "Non-Hispanic Asian",
          "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
          "Hispanic",
          "Non-Hispanic other race"
        )
      ),
    education = dplyr::recode_values(
      EDUCA,
      1:3 ~ "Less than high school",
      4 ~ "High school graduate",
      5 ~ "Some college",
      6 ~ "College graduate",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than high school",
          "High school graduate",
          "Some college",
          "College graduate"
        )
      ),
    employment = dplyr::recode_values(
      EMPLOY1,
      1:2 ~ "Employed",
      3:4 ~ "Out of work",
      5:6 ~ "Homemaker or student",
      7 ~ "Retired",
      8 ~ "Unable to work",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Employed",
          "Out of work",
          "Homemaker or student",
          "Retired",
          "Unable to work"
        )
      ),
    state = factor(`_STATE`),
    # 0/1 outcomes for the models. `==` keeps missing values missing (`%in%` would not).
    diabetes_yes = as.integer(diabetes == "Yes"),
    fair_poor = as.integer(genhlth == "Fair" | genhlth == "Poor")
  ) |>
  # PSU codes repeat across strata: number each stratum-PSU pair.
  tidylog::mutate(psu_id = dplyr::cur_group_id(), .by = c(`_STSTR`, `_PSU`))

WarningA common trap with missing values



genhlth %in% c("Fair", "Poor") returns FALSE (not NA) when genhlth is missing, so everyone with a missing answer would be counted as being in good health. Comparisons with == keep missing values missing.








NoteWhy a new PSU identifier?



In BRFSS, PSU codes are only unique within a stratum: PSU 1 in one stratum is a different phone number from PSU 1 in another. survey::svydesign() can combine them itself (nest = TRUE). Numbering each stratum-PSU pair once gives globally unique integer IDs and avoids repeated relabeling and a large nesting cross-tabulation. The speed difference depends on the installed survey backend; the weights, strata and clusters are unchanged. There are 457,670 pairs for 457,670 respondents: in BRFSS each respondent is their own PSU.

title: 2  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
2.4 Step 4: Check the recoding
The unmatched = "error" arguments already guarantee that every code was mapped. Four more checks confirm the rules we rely on later, including that every PSU identifier sits in a single stratum, which lets the survey designs in later chapters skip their own (slow) check of the same thing.


Code
# Check: the "only during pregnancy" answers are now "No", and the 0/1 outcomes are
# missing exactly where the outcomes are.
stopifnot(
  all(brfss_clean$diabetes[brfss_clean$DIABETE4 %in% 2] == "No"),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes_yes), is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes)),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$fair_poor), is.na(brfss_clean$genhlth))
)
# Check: each PSU identifier belongs to exactly one stratum (PSUs are nested in strata).
stopifnot(
  nrow(dplyr::distinct(brfss_clean, psu_id, `_STSTR`)) ==
    dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id)
)


A crosswalk lists every raw code next to the value it became, with the number of respondents. It is the record of the recoding, and Appendix A shows it in full. Here is income:


Code
recoded <- c(
  DIABETE4 = "diabetes",
  GENHLTH = "genhlth",
  MEDCOST1 = "cost_barrier",
  INCOME3 = "income",
  `_AGE_G` = "age_group",
  `_AGE80` = "age",
  SEXVAR = "sex",
  `_IMPRACE` = "race_eth",
  EDUCA = "education",
  EMPLOY1 = "employment"
)
crosswalk <- purrr::imap(recoded, \(new, item) {
  return(dplyr::count(
    brfss_clean,
    code = as.numeric(.data[[item]]),
    value = as.character(.data[[new]])
  ))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "item")

text:
3.1 The survey design object
Descriptive statistics answer “what does the population look like?” With a complex survey, every estimate has to use the survey design, or it describes the sample (who happened to answer the phone) rather than the population (US adults). This chapter describes the observed data only: the answers people gave, with missing answers shown as missing. Imputed values (Chapter 4) are for models, not for describing who answered what.
The srvyr package lets us describe the design once and then use familiar dplyr verbs on it. The design object stores the data together with the three design features from Chapter 1:
Code
# Check again when reading a saved file: identifiers are nested and weights are valid.

  all(is.finite(brfss_clean$weight)),
  all(brfss_clean$weight > 0),
  nrow(dplyr::distinct(brfss_clean, psu_id, strata)) ==
    dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id)
)
design <- brfss_clean |>
  srvyr::as_survey_design(
    ids = psu_id,
    strata = strata,
    weights = weight,
    nest = FALSE,
    check_strata = FALSE
  )

TipWhy check_strata = FALSE?



By default the design checks that every PSU lies within a single stratum. Depending on the survey package version, this check can create a large PSU-by-stratum table. The psu_id variable numbers each stratum-PSU pair, so the PSUs are nested in strata by construction. Without weights, estimates describe the sample, not the population. Groups that answer surveys more often (older adults, for example) count too much.

The expensive summary chunks below use Quarto’s built-in R cache:

3.7.1 Weights change the estimate

3.7.2 The design changes the uncertainty
The design effect (DEFF) compares the variance of an estimate under the survey design with its variance under a simple random sample of the same size:
\[
\text{DEFF} = \frac{\text{Variance}_\text{survey design}}{\text{Variance}_\text{simple random sample}},
\qquad
n_\text{effective} = \frac{n}{\text{DEFF}}
\]
A DEFF of 2 means the survey gives as much information as a simple random sample half its size, and standard errors are \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4\) times larger.

  dplyr::summarise(
    diabetes = srvyr::survey_mean(diabetes_yes, na.rm = TRUE, deff = TRUE),
    n_diabetes = srvyr::unweighted(sum(!is.na(diabetes_yes))),
    fair_poor = srvyr::survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, deff = TRUE),
    n_fair_poor = srvyr::unweighted(sum(!is.na(fair_poor)))

  dplyr::mutate(
    n_effective_diabetes = n_diabetes / diabetes_deff,

ImportantThree kinds of missing data




Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to anything. Dropping incomplete answers loses precision but does not bias estimates.
Missing at random (MAR): missingness depends on observed variables (here, age and health). Dropping incomplete answers can bias estimates; multiple imputation that includes those variables does not.
Missing not at random (MNAR): missingness depends on the missing value itself (for example, people with very high incomes declining to say). Neither approach fixes this on its own; it calls for sensitivity analyses.

Income missingness varies with age and health, so MCAR is not plausible. Chapter 4 works under MAR, the standard assumption for multiple imputation.

title: 4  Multiple Imputation
text:
4.1 Why not just drop incomplete answers?
Most R modeling functions silently drop every respondent with a missing value in any model variable. Household income is missing for 19.1% of respondents, so a model of diabetes by income would lose about one adult in five. Chapter 3 showed that the people who do not report income are older, in worse health, and more likely to have diabetes than those who do. Dropping them loses precision and can bias the results.
Multiple imputation keeps everyone. It works in three steps:
We use the mice package (multivariate imputation by chained equations), which imputes one variable at a time from the others and cycles through them until the imputations stabilize.

title: 4  Multiple Imputation
text:
Impute. Fill in each missing value with a plausible value drawn from a model that predicts it from everything else we know about the person. Do this several times (here, 5 times) to create 5 completed datasets. The imputed values differ between datasets, and that difference expresses our uncertainty about the true values.
Analyze. Fit the same model to each completed dataset (Chapter 5, Chapter 6).
Pool. Combine the 5 results with Rubin’s rules into one estimate and one standard error that includes the uncertainty from imputation.

title: 4  Multiple Imputation
text:
4.2 The data to impute
We impute the outcomes, the exposure, the covariates, and the two auxiliary variables (education and employment). Auxiliary variables are not in any model, but they predict income well, which makes the imputations more accurate and the “missing at random” assumption more plausible.

title: 4  Multiple Imputation
section: 4.3 Making the imputation model reflect the survey design
text:
4.3 Making the imputation model reflect the survey design
Imputation models are regression models. If they ignore the survey design, the imputed values reflect the sample, and later weighted estimates can be biased. The practical recommendation (Reiter, Raghunathan, and Kinney, 2006) is to use the design variables as predictors:

the weight is a predictor, so imputed values can vary with it;
the strata and PSU identifiers have thousands of values (and one PSU per person), so they cannot be predictors. They stay in the data, untouched, for the survey design in the next chapters;
the state can represent geographic differences, but its 53 categories add parameters to each imputation model. This teaching example omits state from the default predictor matrix. title: 4  Multiple Imputation
text:
4.4 How each variable is imputed
We impute every variable with predictive mean matching (PMM). For each person with a missing value, PMM predicts the value from a regression, finds the respondents with an observed value whose predictions are closest, and copies the observed value of one of them, chosen at random. Imputed values are therefore always real answers (an income group, never “2.4”), and PMM is fast: one linear regression per variable.


Code

An empty string means the variable has nothing missing.






NotePMM or a model for each type of variable?



mice’s defaults model each categorical variable by its type: logistic regression for two categories, proportional-odds regression for ordered ones, and multinomial regression for unordered ones. This teaching example uses PMM for all incomplete variables to keep the workflow compact. When adapting it, choose methods appropriate to each variable’s measurement scale, inspect the imputations and compare alternatives. A small proportion of missing values alone does not establish that a method is appropriate. Always report the method used for each variable.

title: 4  Multiple Imputation
text:
4.5 Imputing in parallel, reproducibly
Each completed dataset is independent of the others, so they can be imputed at the same time on different processor cores. furrr::future_map() runs one imputation per task, and mice::ibind() combines the single imputations into one object. future::plan() sets the number of parallel workers. First detect the available cores; reserve one core and use at most four workers, or fewer if there are fewer imputations. The cap limits memory use because each worker holds its own data.
The main example uses 5 imputations to keep a classroom run short. For a substantive analysis, assess the fraction of missing information and the stability of pooled estimates and standard errors, and increase the number of imputations when needed.
The seed argument makes the results reproducible. furrr gives each task its own random-number stream derived from the seed, so the imputations are identical on every computer, whatever its number of cores. (mice::futuremice() also imputes in parallel, but its results depend on the number of cores.)

title: 5  Bivariate Models
text:
5.1 Prevalence ratios
A bivariate (or “crude”, or “unadjusted”) model relates the outcome to one variable at a time. Crude associations describe the population; they are not causal effects, because other variables are not held constant. Chapter 6 adjusts for them.
Our outcome is whether an adult has ever been told they have diabetes (1 = yes, 0 = no or prediabetes). We compare the prevalence of diabetes between groups:
\[
\text{PR} = \frac{\text{prevalence of diabetes in a group}}{\text{prevalence of diabetes in the reference group}}
\]
A PR of 2 means the group has twice the prevalence of the reference group. A Poisson regression with a log link and a 0/1 outcome estimates prevalence ratios directly (“modified Poisson” regression): its exponentiated coefficients are PRs. Two details:

title: 5  Bivariate Models
text:
We use family = quasipoisson() rather than poisson(), because survey weights are not whole numbers. The estimates are the same.
A Poisson model’s own standard errors are wrong for a 0/1 outcome, but survey::svyglm() does not use them: it computes design-based (robust) standard errors from the weights, strata, and PSUs.







TipWhy not odds ratios?



Logistic regression estimates odds ratios. When an outcome is common, as diabetes is (about one adult in eight), odds ratios are further from 1 than prevalence ratios and are easily misread as “times as likely”. Prevalence ratios mean what they say.

For each coefficient, Rubin’s rules combine the 5 results on the log scale (the estimate column above is already exponentiated into a PR):

6.3 Does income matter overall?
Income has four groups, so it has three PRs, each with its own p-value. To ask whether income is associated with diabetes at all, we test the three coefficients together (null hypothesis: all three are zero on the log scale). mitml::testConstraints() runs this multivariate Wald test across imputations (the “D1” statistic, pooled with Rubin’s rules) from each dataset’s estimates and covariance matrix.

income_test <- mitml::testConstraints(
  qhat = do.call(cbind, purrr::map(adjusted_fits, "coef")),
  uhat = simplify2array(purrr::map(adjusted_fits, \(fit) fit$vcov)),
  constraints = paste0("`", income_terms, "`"), # backticks: the names contain spaces
  method = "D1"
)

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.1 The same packages: renv
Anyone who runs this book should get the same numbers. Three things make that possible.
R packages change between versions, and a new version can change a result. The renv package records the exact version of every package the book uses in renv.lock and installs those versions into a library inside the project (renv/library/), separate from your other R projects.
renv starts automatically when R opens in the project folder (through the .Rprofile file). The packages the book needs are listed in DESCRIPTION; renv records them and their dependencies.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
section: B.2 The same random numbers: seeds
text:
B.2 The same random numbers: seeds
Multiple imputation draws random values. _common.R sets the same seed (2024) at the start of every chapter. The imputation runs one task per imputation in parallel, and furrr::furrr_options(seed = seed) gives each task its own reproducible random-number stream, so the imputed values are the same whether your computer has 2 cores or 16.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.3 Smoke tests
A full render takes time because of the imputation. Before a full run, a smoke test checks that every chapter works:
quarto render book --profile smoke
The smoke profile (_quarto-smoke.yml and _environment-smoke) sets the number of imputations to 2 and writes the book to book/_book-smoke/ and the data to data/processed-smoke/. Every page of a smoke book says “SMOKE TEST” in its title. The number of imputations is set in one place (N_IMPUTATIONS, read in _common.R), and every count in the code and text follows it.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.4 Reusing expensive calculations
Expensive R chunks use #| cache: true, Quarto’s standard knitr cache. The setup records the chapter’s R code, contents of its input files, shared settings, R/package versions and survey options in cache.extra. These inputs invalidate cached results when the analysis changes. Editing prose does not.
Full runs store their caches in data/processed/cache/; smoke runs use data/processed-smoke/cache/. Setup and file-saving chunks always run, so later chapters still receive their inputs on a cached render. Only rendering uses the cache; running individual lines in the R console executes them normally.
To recalculate all cached chunks:
quarto render book --cache-refresh
Or refresh only the descriptive chapter:
quarto render book/03-descriptives.qmd --cache-refresh
See the Quarto caching documentation for details. Validate the initial calculation before relying on cached results.
